Platform lead, mid-market logistics

Most assessments describe a system. Yours has to decide something.

A readiness score tells a steering committee how it feels. An ordered list of insertion points, each with the file it touches and the effort it costs, tells an engineering team what to do on Monday. We only ship the second kind.

How the read works

Three passes over the same repository, each one narrowing what the next has to look at.

01

Facts before opinions

Dependency graph, entry points, data stores, external calls. Nothing interpretive until the inventory is complete.

02

Lenses in parallel

Architecture, security, observability, and AI opportunity each run against the same facts, independently.

Six lenses

Each one answers a question a different person in the room is asking.

AI opportunity

Where the system could carry a model, ranked by impact against effort, with the insertion point named in code rather than described in the abstract.

Architecture

Container and component views generated from source, so the diagram matches the repository instead of last year's whiteboard.

Security posture

Secrets, authz gaps, unsafe patterns, dependency hygiene. Severity-ranked, evidence-cited.

Observability

Whether anyone could tell this system was failing before a customer did.

Vertical slice

One real user action followed from the click to the data store and back, with the gap at every hop flagged.

Modernization order

What to do first, and what it is safe to leave alone. The order is the deliverable.

The order matters more than the list

Nearly every team we meet already has a list. It came out of a retro, or an incident, or a vendor conversation, and everything on it is defensible. What the list does not have is an order, which is why it has not moved in nine months.

Sequencing is the deliverable. The inventory is just how you earn the right to sequence.

So the assessment spends its last pass doing the unglamorous thing: deciding what is cheapest to do that unlocks the most of what comes after. Typography before layout, in design terms. Instrumentation before optimization, in ours.

Where it has run

  • Logistics

    Route planner

    Legacy monolith, no tracing, three teams sharing one deploy.

  • Health

    Intake portal

    Compliance-bound, so every insertion point needed a data-handling note.

  • Fintech

    Ledger service

    Well observed, badly documented. The diagram was the whole value.

  • Retail

    Storefront

    Inherited from an agency, then extended by four contractors.

  • Industrial

    Telemetry

    High volume, low signal. Metrics existed, alerts did not.

  • Media

    Asset pipeline

    Batch jobs nobody owned. Ownership map came out of the recon pass.

  • SaaS

    Admin console

    The vertical slice found two hops nobody knew were synchronous.

  • Public

    Permit intake

    Accessibility was the constraint that ordered everything else.
